--- title: "Feature importance" description: "A random forest has no coefficients to read, but shuffling one input at a time shows how much its predictions rely on each. Inputs that carry the same information share the credit, so a score depends on which other inputs the model had." order: 1 categories: [interpretation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Importance scores say which inputs a model relies on Once a model is fitted, the first question is usually which inputs it uses. A linear model answers through its coefficients: one number for each input, in the outcome's units. A random forest averages hundreds of trees and has no such numbers. **Feature importance** gives every input a score for how much a fitted model relies on it, and works for any model. This page shows the most widely used score, and why a score depends on the other inputs the model was given. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Permutation importance shuffles an input and measures the rise in error **Permutation importance** works on any fitted model. Predict the test data and measure the error, here the [RMSE](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#rmse-measures-a-typical-miss-on-the-test-stations). Then shuffle one input: mix up its values, so each row gets another row's value. The input's values are all still there, but they no longer belong to their rows. If the model relied on that input, its predictions get worse and the error rises; if it did not, the error stays about the same. The rise is the input's importance. ::: {.diagram} ![Permutation importance in three steps: score the test data as it is, shuffle one input so its values change rows, and score again. The rise in error is the input's importance.](img/permutation-importance.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Score, the test data as it is: a small table with inputs A, B and C and an outcome column, each cell shaded, and the text predict the test data and measure the error. Shuffle one input, its values change rows: the same table with column B outlined in orange and its shades in a different order, labelled shuffled, and the text mix up the input's values, so they no longer belong to their rows. Score again, the rise is the importance: two error bars, before and after, with the after bar taller and the extra part marked as the rise. A note says repeat for each input, several times over, on data the model was not fitted to."} ::: Shuffling is random, so it is repeated several times and the rises are averaged. It is done on test data, so the score is about predicting new sites. A category such as substrate is shuffled as one column, so it gets one score. Random forests also report a built-in score from their own splits on the training data; this course uses permutation importance, which means the same thing for every model. ## Inputs that carry the same information share their importance Two inputs that rise and fall together, with a high [correlation](../02-marine-data/the-coastal-survey.qmd), tell a model much the same thing. A model fitted with both can lean on either, and splits the work between them. Shuffling one then costs it little, because the other still carries most of the information, so each scores lower than it would alone. Fit the model without one of them and the other takes over its work, and its score rises. So an importance score belongs to a model **and its set of inputs**. A low score does not mean an input is unrelated to the outcome; it may mean another input already told the model the same thing. ## Worked example A random forest of 500 trees, as in [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), predicts abundance from the six inputs of [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd): depth, temperature, chlorophyll, salinity, substrate and season. It is fitted to the training sites of one split by site and scored on its test sites, then fitted again without temperature. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") modelling <- survey |> select(site_id, abundance, all_of(inputs)) split <- group_initial_split(modelling, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) forest_recipe <- function(data) { recipe(abundance ~ ., data = data) |> update_role(site_id, new_role = "site") |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) } forest_model <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] test = survey.iloc[test_rows] def new_forest(numeric, categorical): recipe = ColumnTransformer( [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical)], verbose_feature_names_out=False) # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] ``` ::: ::: ### Temperature is the input the forest relies on most Each input is shuffled 20 times on the test sites, and its importance is the average rise in RMSE. Substrate and season are shuffled as whole columns, before the recipe turns them into levels. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the rise in test RMSE when an input is shuffled, averaged over the shuffles shuffle_importance <- function(fitted, data, repeats = 20) { error <- \(d) rmse_vec(d$abundance, predict(fitted, d)$.pred) before <- error(data) columns <- setdiff(names(data), c("site_id", "abundance")) map(columns, \(input) { rises <- map_dbl(seq_len(repeats), \(i) { shuffled <- data shuffled[[input]] <- sample(shuffled[[input]]) error(shuffled) - before }) tibble(input, rise = mean(rises)) }) |> list_rbind() } forest <- workflow(forest_recipe(train), forest_model) |> fit(train) all_six <- shuffle_importance(forest, test) all_six |> arrange(desc(rise)) |> mutate(rise = round(rise, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|input | rise| |:-----------------|------:| |temperature_c | 0.340| |depth_m | 0.101| |substrate | 0.084| |season | 0.044| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 0.002| |salinity_psu | -0.014|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # permutation_importance shuffles each column of the data it is given, so # substrate and season are shuffled whole, before the recipe. Its score is # minus the RMSE, so a rise in error is a positive importance. def shuffle_importance(fitted, data, columns, repeats=20): result = permutation_importance( fitted, data[columns], data["abundance"], n_repeats=repeats, random_state=123, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") return pd.DataFrame({"input": columns, "rise": result.importances_mean}) forest = new_forest(numeric, categorical).fit( train[numeric + categorical], train["abundance"]) all_six = shuffle_importance(forest, test, numeric + categorical) (all_six.sort_values("rise", ascending=False) .round(3) .reset_index(drop=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | input | rise | |:------------------|-------:| | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 0.406 | | temperature_c | 0.287 | | depth_m | 0.194 | | season | 0.1 | | substrate | 0.077 | | salinity_psu | 0.025 | ::: ::: ::: The forest's test RMSE is 3.93 individuals. Shuffling temperature raises it by 0.340, 3.4 times as much as shuffling depth, the next input. Chlorophyll and salinity barely move it: shuffled, they cost the forest almost nothing. The Python tab, with its own split of the sites, ranks chlorophyll above temperature. ### Without temperature the forest leans on season instead The forest is fitted again to the same training sites with temperature left out, and scored and shuffled on the same test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_five <- select(train, -temperature_c) test_five <- select(test, -temperature_c) forest_five <- workflow(forest_recipe(train_five), forest_model) |> fit(train_five) without <- shuffle_importance(forest_five, test_five) errors <- tibble( inputs = c("All six", "Without temperature"), rmse = c(rmse_vec(test$abundance, predict(forest, test)$.pred), rmse_vec(test$abundance, predict(forest_five, test_five)$.pred))) errors |> mutate(rmse = round(rmse, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|inputs | rmse| |:-------------------|----:| |All six | 3.93| |Without temperature | 4.01|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} five = ["depth_m", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] forest_five = new_forest(five, categorical).fit( train[five + categorical], train["abundance"]) without = shuffle_importance(forest_five, test, five + categorical) pd.DataFrame({ "inputs": ["All six", "Without temperature"], "rmse": [root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], forest.predict(test[numeric + categorical])), root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], forest_five.predict(test[five + categorical]))] }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | inputs | rmse | |:--------------------|-------:| | All six | 4.74 | | Without temperature | 4.84 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_rows("All six inputs" = all_six, "Without temperature" = without, .id = "forest") |> # the first level is drawn lowest, so the forest with all six inputs comes last mutate(forest = factor(forest, levels = c("Without temperature", "All six inputs")), input = str_to_sentence(input_names[input]), input = factor(input, levels = rev(str_to_sentence(input_names[ranked])))) |> ggplot(aes(rise, input, fill = forest)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge(preserve = "single"), width = 0.75) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.4) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("All six inputs" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Without temperature" = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) + labs(x = "Rise in test RMSE when shuffled (individuals)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Permutation importance on the test sites, for the forest with all six inputs and for the forest fitted without temperature. Without temperature, season's importance rises several times over.](feature-importance_files/figure-html/fig-shared-1.png){#fig-shared fig-alt='Horizontal bars, one row for each input, two bars per row: the forest with all six inputs in blue and the forest without temperature in orange, the rise in test RMSE when shuffled on the horizontal axis. Temperature has a long blue bar, 0.340, and no orange bar. Season grows from 0.044 in blue to 0.153 in orange. The other inputs change little.' width=1500} ::: ::: Left out altogether, temperature costs the forest only 0.08 in RMSE, from 3.93 to 4.01, far less than the 0.340 that shuffling it cost. Season does the work instead: its importance rises from 0.044 to 0.153 (@fig-shared). Summer water is warm and winter water cold, so season carries much of what temperature told the forest. With both inputs, temperature took the credit; without temperature, season does. ## Importance shows what a model uses, not what the species needs A high score means the fitted model leans on that input to predict. A low score means the model managed without it, which can happen because another input carries the same information, as season did for temperature. Scores also say nothing about the direction or shape of an effect, whether abundance rises or falls with temperature. [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) draws that shape. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Feature importance** scores how much a fitted model relies on each input, for any model. - **Permutation importance** shuffles one input on test data and measures the rise in error: on the survey, temperature mattered most to the forest. - **Inputs that carry the same information share their importance.** Without temperature, the forest leaned on season, and lost little accuracy. - A score belongs to a model and its set of inputs. It says what the model uses, not the direction of an effect or its cause. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Leave depth out instead of temperature. Which inputs take over its work, and how much does the RMSE change? 2. Swap the random forest for boosted trees (`boost_tree()` with the `xgboost` engine). Does temperature still lead?
